¶
'''bequeath†''' (bẹ̄-kwēᴛ̵ʜ′), ''n.'' [< ''bequeath'', ''v.''] A bequest.

'''bequeathable''' (bẹ̄-kwē′ᴛ̵ʜạ-bl), ''a.'' [< ''bequeath'' + ''-able.''] Capable of being bequeathed.

'''bequeathal''' (bẹ̄-kwē′ᴛ̵ʜạl), ''n.'' [< ''bequeath'' + ''-al.''] The act of bequeathing; bequest.
{{smaller block|The ''bequeathal'' of their savings may be a means of giving unalloyed happiness.
{{right|''The American'', VI. 324.}}}}

'''bequeather''' (bẹ̄-kwē′ᴛ̵ʜėr), ''n.'' One who bequeaths.

'''bequeathment''' (bẹ̄-kwēᴛ̵ʜ′ment), ''n.'' [< ''bequeath'' + ''-ment.''] The act of bequeathing; a bequest.

'''bequest''' (bẹ̄-kwest′), ''n.'' [< ME. ''bequeste'', ''byquyste'', prob. (with excrescent ''-t'', as in ''behest'', and shifted accent, after the verb) < AS. *''bīcwis'' (equiv. to ''bīcwide'', ME. ''bequide'', after ''becwethan'', ME. ''bequethen''),< ''bī-'', accented form, in nouns, of ''bi-'', ''be-'', + ''cwis'' (''cwiss-''), saying, < ''cwethan'', say: see ''bequeath''.] '''1.''' The act of bequeathing or leaving by will.
{{smaller block|He claimed the crown to himself, pretending an adoption, or ''bequest'' of the kingdom unto him, by the Confessor.
{{right|''Sir M. Hale.''}}
Possession, with the right of ''bequest'' and inheritance, is the stimulant which raises property to its highest value.
{{right|''N. A. Rev.'', CXLIII. 58.}}}}
'''2.''' That which is left by will; a legacy.—'''3.''' That which is or has been handed down or transmitted.
{{smaller block|Our cathedrals, our creeds, our liturgies, our varied ministries of compassion for every form of human suffering, are a ''bequest'' from the age of faith.
{{right|''H. N. Oxenham'', Short Studies, p. 263.}}}}

¶
'''bequest†''' (bē-kwest′), ''v. t.'' [< ''bequest, n.''] To give as a bequest; bequeath.

'''bequethe†,''' ''v. t.'' An obsolete form of ''bequeath. Chaucer.''

'''bequia-sweet''' (bā-kē′ä-swēt), ''n.'' [See quot.] An oscine passerine bird, of the family ''Icteridæ'' and subfamily ''Quiscalinæ;'' the ''Quiscalus luminosus'', a grakle found in the Caribbees: so named from its note.
{{smaller block|In Bequia [in the Caribbees], and extending throughout the chain [of islands], is a blackbird, a new species named the ''Quiscalus luminosus'', which makes the air resound with its joyous cry: “''Bequia sweet, sweet, Bequia sweet.''”
{{right|''Ober'', Camps in the Caribbees, p. 246.}}}}

'''bequote''' (bē-kwōt′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''quote.''] To quote frequently or much.

'''beraft†,''' ''pp.'' A Middle English past participle of ''bereave.''

'''berain†''' (bē-rān′), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''beraynen, bereinen'' (= OHG. ''bireganōn'', G. ''beregnen''), < ''be-'' + ''reinen'', rain: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''rain''<sup>1</sup>.] To rain upon.
{{smaller block|With his teris salt hire breest ''byreyned.''
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 1172.}}}}

'''Berardius''' (be-rär′di-us), ''n.'' [NL., named after M. ''Bérard.''] A genus of odontocete whales, of the family ''Physeteridæ'' and subfamily ''Ziphiinæ'', having two functional teeth on each side of the mandibular symphysis. {{smaller|It is related in general characters to ''Ziphius'' and ''Mesoplodon.'' The only species, ''B. arnouxi'', attaining a length of about 30 feet, is found in New Zealand waters.}}

'''Berard steel.''' See ''steel.''

¶
'''berat''' (be-rat′), ''n.'' [Armen.] A warrant or patent of dignity or privilege given by an Oriental monarch.

'''berate''' (bẹ̄-rāt′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''rate''<sup>2</sup>.] To chide vehemently; scold.
{{smaller block|Zopyrus ''berated'' Socrates as if he had caught a pickpocket.
{{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XXII. 65.}}}}

'''berattle†''' (bẹ̄-rat′l), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''rattle.''] To cry down; abuse; run down. ''Shak.'' [Rare.]

'''beraunite''' (be-râ′nīt), ''n.'' [< ''Beraun'' (see def.) + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.] A hydrous phosphate of iron of a reddish-brown color, found at St. Benigna near Beraun in Bohemia.

'''beray†''' (bẹ̄-rā′), ''v. t.'' [< ''be-''<sup>1</sup> + ''ray''<sup>3</sup>.] '''1.''' To make foul; defile; soil.
{{smaller block|''Beraying'' the font and water while the bishop was baptizing him.
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., vi.}}}}
'''2.''' To scent.
{{smaller block|<poem>How comes your handkercher
So sweetly thus ''beray’d?''</poem>
{{right|''Middleton'', The Witch, i. 2.}}}}

'''berbe''' (bėrb), ''n.'' The name of an African genet, ''Genetta pardina.''

'''Berber''' (bėr′bėr), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< Ar. ''Berber'', ''Barbar'', the Berbers: see ''barbary'' and ''barb''<sup>3</sup>.] '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A person belonging to any one of a group of tribes inhabiting the mountainous parts of Barbary and portions of the Sahara, descended from the primitive race of those regions.—'''2.''' The language spoken by the Berbers. It is one of the Hamitic languages.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to the Berbers or their language.

'''Berberidaceæ''' (bėr″be-ri-dā′sẹ̄-ē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Berberis'' (''Berberid-'') + ''-aceæ''.] A natural order of plants, belonging to the thalamifloral dicotyledons, distinguished from allied orders by having the few stamens in two or three whorls and the anthers opening by valves. {{smaller|The genera are widely distributed, but are small, with the exception of ''Berberis''. Of the smaller genera, the blue cohosh (''Caulophyllum''), the mandrake (''Podophyllum''), and the twin-leaf (''Jeffersonia'') are of more or less repute in medicine, and the ''Akebia'' is an ornamental climber. See cut under ''Berberis''.}}

'''berberidaceous''' (bėr″be-ri-dā′shius), ''a.'' Of or pertaining to the ''Berberidaceæ''.

'''berberine''' (bėr′be-rin), ''n.'' [< NL. ''berberina'': see ''Berberis'' and ''-ine''<sup>2</sup>.] An alkaloid (C<sub>20</sub>H<sub>17</sub>NO<sub>4</sub>) widely distributed in the vegetable kingdom, being found in the barberry and a considerable number of plants, or parts of plants, whose extracts combine a yellow color and bit-

bark of the barberry. It is an amorphous white powder, bitter to the taste.

'''berceuse''' (bār-sėz′), ''n.'' [F., a rocker, a lullaby. Cf. ''berceau'', a cradle, < ''bercer'', rock, lull to sleep.] A cradle-song; especially, a vocal or instrumental composition of a tender, quiet, and soothing character.

'''bercheroot''' (ber′che-röt), ''n.'' The Russian pound, the unit of weight in Russia. The standard of 1835 equals 409.5174 grams, or 0.9028307 of a pound avoirdupois.

'''bercowetz''', ''n.'' See ''berkovets''.

¶
'''berdash†''', ''n.'' See ''burdash.''

'''berde†''', ''n.'' An obsolete form of ''beard.''

'''bere<sup>1</sup>†''', ''v.'', '''bere<sup>2</sup>†''', ''n.'', etc. An obsolete form of ''bear''<sup>1</sup>, ''bear''<sup>2</sup>, etc., ''berry''<sup>4</sup>, etc.

'''Berean''' (bē-rē′an), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [Also written ''Beræan'', < L. ''Beræus'', < ''Beræa'', < Gr. Βέροια, Βέρροια.] '''I.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to the ancient town of Berea (Berœa, now Verria) in Macedonia; in religious use, resembling the people of Berea as described in the Acts. See II., 2.

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' An inhabitant of ancient Berea.—'''2.''' One of a sect of dissenters from the Church of Scotland, who took their name from and profess to follow the ancient Bereans mentioned in Acts xvii. 11, in building their system of faith and practice upon the Scriptures alone, without regard to human authority. Also called ''Barclayites'', from their founder, John Barclay (1734–98), of Muthill, Perthshire.

'''Berea sandstone.''' See ''sandstone.''

'''bereave''' (bē-rēv′), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''bereaved'' or ''bereft'', ppr. ''bereaving.'' [< ME. ''bereven'', ''bireven'' (pret. ''berevede'', ''berefte'', ''bereft'', ''berafte'', pp. ''bereved'', ''bereft'', ''beraft''), < AS. ''bereáfian'' (= OFries. ''birāva'' = OS. ''birōbhōn'' = D. ''berooven'' = OHG. ''biroubōn'', MHG. ''berouben'', G. ''berauben'' = Goth. ''biraubōn''), rob, bereave, < ''be-'' + ''reáfian'', plunder, rob: see ''be-''<sup>1</sup> and ''reave.''] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To deprive by or as if by violence; rob; strip: with ''of'' before the thing taken away.
{{smaller block|Me have ye ''bereaved of'' my children. {{right|Gen. xlii. 36.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Fate had weaven
The twist of life, and her ''of'' life ''bereaven.''</poem>
{{right|''Ford'', Fame’s Memorial.}}}}

'''Berengarian''' (ber-en-gā′ri-a̤n), ''n.'' and ''a.'' [< ML. ''Berengarius'', Berengar, a theologian, born about {{sc|a. d.}} 998, died about 1088.] '''I.''' ''n.'' One of a sect which followed Berengarius or Berengar of Tours, archdeacon of Angers in the eleventh century, who denied the doctrine of transubstantiation.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to the Berengarians or their opinions.

'''Berengarianism''' (ber-en-gā′ri-a̤n-izm), ''n.'' [< ''Berengarian'' + ''-ism''.] The opinions or doctrines of Berengarius and his followers. See ''Berengarian''.

'''Berenice’s hair.''' See ''Coma Berenices''.

'''beresite''' (ber′e-sīt), ''n.'' [< ''Beres''(''ovsk'') + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.] A fine-grained granite found near Beresovsk, Russia, in the Ural, associated with gold-bearing quartz.

'''beret, berret'''<sup>1</sup> (ber′et), ''n.'' [F. ''béret'', < ML. ''beretta'', ''biretta'', a cap: see ''barret''<sup>2</sup> and ''biretta''.] '''1.''' A round flat woolen cap worn by the Basque peasantry. ''N. E. D.''—'''2.''' Same as ''biretta''.

'''beretta''', ''n.'' See ''biretta''.

'''berettina''', ''n.'' See ''berrettina''.

'''berewick†''', ''n.'' See ''berwick''.

'''berg'''<sup>1</sup> (bėrg), ''n.'' [< Icel. Sw. Norw. ''berg'' = Dan. ''bjerg'', a rock, G. ''berg'' = E. ''barrow''<sup>1</sup>, a hill.] A rock. [Shetland.]

'''berg'''<sup>2</sup> (bėrg), ''n.'' [From ''-berg'' in ''iceberg'', < G. ''eisberg'': see ''iceberg''. Not from AS. ''beorg'', a hill, which gives E. ''barrow''<sup>1</sup>, a mound (but cf. ''bergh''): see ''barrow''<sup>1</sup>.] A large floating mass or mountain of ice; an iceberg.
{{smaller block|Like glittering ''bergs'' of ice.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, iv.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|bequeath|528|berg}}</noinclude>remains archaically in an idiomatic construction (see ''quoth''). The compound has been preserved through its technical use in wills.] '''1†.''' To give away; transfer the possession of; assign as a gift.
{{smaller block|<poem>Wilt thou forsake thy fortune,
''Bequeath'' thy land to him, and follow me?</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', K. John, i. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' To give or leave by will; assign as a legacy: more commonly, but not necessarily, used of personal property, in contradistinction to real property, which is said to be ''devised''.
{{smaller block|<poem>Mine heritage,
Which my dead father did ''bequeath'' to me.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, ii. 1.}}}}
'''3.''' To hand down; transmit.
{{smaller block|One generation has ''bequeathed'' its religious gloom and the counterfeit of its religious ardor to the next.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Main Street.}}}}
{{smaller block|Greece has ''bequeathed'' to us her ever living tongue, and the immortal productions of her intellect.
{{right|''Gladstone'', Might of Right, p. 16.}}}}
'''4†.''' To commit; commend; intrust.
{{smaller block|<poem>We to flames our slaughtered friends ''bequeath''.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, vii. 399.}}}}
'''5†.''' To give or yield; furnish; impart.
{{smaller block|A niggards purse shall scarce ''bequeath'' his master a good dinner.
''Pennyless Parl.'', in Harl. Misc. (Malh.), III. 72. (''N. E. D.'')
That which ''bequeaths'' it this slow pace.
{{right|''N. Fairfax'', Bulk and Selv., p. 122. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}
'''6†.''' Reflexively, to commit; dedicate; devote.
{{smaller block|Orpheus . . . ''bequeaths himself'' to a solitary life in the deserts.
{{right|''K. Digby'', Broad Stone of Honour, I. 166. (''N. E. D.'')}}}}

''Of'' name and honor?</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 18.}}}}
{{smaller block|[It is sometimes used without ''of'', more especially in the passive, the subject of the verb being either the person deprived or the thing taken away.
<poem>And ’tis your fault I am ''bereft'' him so.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Venus and Adonis, l. 381.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>All your interest in those territories
Is utterly ''bereft'' you. ''Shak.'', 2 Hen. VI., iii. 1.]</poem>}}
'''2†.''' To take away by destroying, impairing, or spoiling; take away by violence.
{{smaller block|Shall move you to ''bereave'' my life. {{right|''Marlowe.''}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I think his understanding is ''bereft.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', 3 Hen. VI., ii. 6.}}}}
'''3†.''' To deprive of power; prevent.
{{smaller block|<poem>No thing may ''bireve''
A man to love, til that him list to leve.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 685.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To destroy life; cut off. [Rare.]

'''bereavement''' (bẹ̄-rēv′ment), ''n.''   [< ''bereave'' + ''-ment.'']   '''1.''' The act of bereaving.—'''2.''' The state of being bereaved; grievous loss; particularly, the loss of a relative or friend by death.
{{smaller block|He bore his ''bereavement'' with stoical fortitude.
{{right|''H. Smith'', Tor Hill.}}}}

'''bereaver''' (bẹ̄-rē′vėr), ''n.'' One who bereaves or deprives another of something valued.

'''bereft''' (bẹ̄-reft′). Preterit and past participle of ''bereave''.

'''Berengarian''' (ber-en-gā′ri-a̤n), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [< ML. ''Berengarius'', Berengar, a theologian, born about {{sc|a. d.}} 998, died about 1088.]   '''I.''' ''n.'' One of a sect which followed Berengarius or Berengar of Tours, archdeacon of Angers in the eleventh century, who denied the doctrine of transubstantiation.

'''II.''' ''a.'' Of or pertaining to the Berengarians or their opinions.

'''Berengarianism''' (ber-en-gā′ri-a̤n-izm), ''n.''   [< ''Berengarian'' + ''-ism''.]   The opinions or doctrines of Berengarius and his followers. See ''Berengarian''.

'''Berenice’s hair.''' See ''Coma Berenices''.

'''beresite''' (ber′e-sīt), ''n.''   [< ''Beres''(''ovsk'') + ''-ite''<sup>2</sup>.]   A fine-grained granite found near Beresovsk, Russia, in the Ural, associated with gold-bearing quartz.

'''beret, berret'''<sup>1</sup> (ber′et), ''n.''   [F. ''béret'', < ML. ''beretta'', ''biretta'', a cap: see ''barret''<sup>2</sup> and ''biretta''.]   '''1.''' A round flat woolen cap worn by the Basque peasantry.   ''N. E. D.''—'''2.''' Same as ''biretta''.

'''beretta''', ''n.'' See ''biretta''.

'''berettina''', ''n.'' See ''berrettina''.

'''berewick†''', ''n.'' See ''berwick''.

'''berg'''<sup>1</sup> (bėrg), ''n.''   [< Icel. Sw. Norw. ''berg'' = Dan. ''bjerg'', a rock, G. ''berg'' = E. ''barrow''<sup>1</sup>, a hill.]   A rock. [Shetland.]

'''berg'''<sup>2</sup> (bėrg), ''n.''   [From ''-berg'' in ''iceberg'', < G. ''eisberg'': see ''iceberg''. Not from AS. ''beorg'', a hill, which gives E. ''barrow''<sup>1</sup>, a mound (but cf. ''bergh''): see ''barrow''<sup>1</sup>.]   A large floating mass or mountain of ice; an iceberg.
{{smaller block|Like glittering ''bergs'' of ice.
